column4: A user pastes override instructions into a cart item name; cart contents are inserted verbatim into the prompt allowing the injected text to redirect the model.
column6: No special access needed — any user can add a cart item with crafted text; well-documented vector with no special tooling required.
column8: Exposes system prompt and redirects model output for one session; does not directly leak payment data or affect other users.
column10: Merchant-side variant: a crafted product name injects for every customer who adds that item

column4: The model includes fragments of another customer's cart in the summary response due to context bleed between requests.
column6: Requires a session-isolation implementation bug rather than deliberate attacker input; not trivially exploitable.
column8: Any cross-customer cart exposure is a GDPR breach; at 3M calls/month even a 0.001% rate is 3000 exposures/month.
column10: Amplified by call volume — low per-call probability × high frequency = material expected exposure

column4: An attacker uses a successful T01 injection to extract the full system prompt exposing business logic and constraints.
column6: Chained attack — requires T01 to succeed first; reduces standalone likelihood.
column8: Leaked system prompt enables more targeted future injections but does not directly expose customer data.
column10: Secondary consequence of T01; mitigating T01 reduces this threat

column4: The model generates a cart summary with fabricated prices or quantities causing the customer to confirm an incorrect order.
column6: Hallucination rates for structured data are non-trivial without a ground-truth validation step against the Orders DB.
column8: The summary is informational — actual checkout price is sourced from the Orders DB; misinformation causes confusion and trust erosion but not direct incorrect charges.
column10: No output validation against Orders DB is the enabling gap; impact bounded because the checkout step uses DB data not AI output

column4: An attacker sends a crafted payload that is not sanitised before being assembled into a SQL query allowing read or modification of order records.
column6: Cart input fields are plausible injection points and free tooling (sqlmap) is available; ORMs reduce but do not eliminate risk.
column8: Full read/write access to the Orders DB across all customers — mass PII extraction or data destruction is possible.
column10: Orders DB holds all customer data across 22 countries; exploit tooling freely available

column4: A user accesses another customer's cart summary by manipulating the cart ID because the API does not verify ownership.
column6: BOLA requires only changing an ID in a request — most common API vulnerability (OWASP API1:2023); no special tooling needed.
column8: Each successful request is a separate GDPR-notifiable breach exposing full cart contents and linked PII.
column10: TOP CRITICAL RISK — Blast radius: ~6,000 carts/minute enumerable at 100 req/s bot rate; each cart = name + email + delivery address + full item list; 22 GDPR jurisdictions; notification obligation per breach

column4: The DIAL or Stripe API key is committed to the repository or exposed in build logs giving an attacker ability to make model calls or initiate charges.
column6: CI/CD logs are accessible to all repo contributors and no secret-scan step exists in the pipeline (K 8.W.3 gap).
column8: Leaked Stripe key enables unauthorised charges and refunds; leaked DIAL key enables unbounded model calls at Meridian's expense.
column10: Two separate critical assets at risk from one pipeline gap; Stripe key exposure is a PCI DSS incident

column4: A bot or loop bug fires the /summarise endpoint at high rate exhausting the DIAL AI meter and blocking legitimate users.
column6: No rate limit or retry cap on /summarise (K 8.W.3 Gap 2); unauthenticated endpoint; a loop requires no access.
column8: Exhausting the $18k DIAL hard cap blocks all AI calls for the Checkout tenant and can incur the full cap cost within hours.
column10: Financial DoS — exhausting the cost cap is as damaging as a traffic-based DoS for AI-metered features

column4: An attacker on the internal network intercepts the cart-to-DIAL data flow and reads the prompt payload containing customer PII.
column6: Requires attacker position on the internal network or a misconfigured proxy — not exploitable from outside.
column8: Full prompt payload (cart contents + PII) exposed in transit for every intercepted call.
column10: Risk at the tb_app → tb_ai trust boundary; TLS enforcement is the primary control

column4: A forged Stripe webhook is accepted without signature verification marking an unpaid order as confirmed.
column6: Stripe HMAC webhook forgery is publicly documented; depends on whether signature verification is implemented.
column8: A forged webhook dispatches goods without payment; revenue loss scales with automation.
column10: Standard control (HMAC-SHA256 on Stripe-Signature header) is known; absence is a deployment gap

column4: Any principal with kubectl get secret in the meridian namespace can read the payment-provider API key.
column6: Default K8s RBAC often grants namespace access to platform engineers; no secrets manager in place (K 8.W.2 Gap 3).
column8: Stripe key extraction has same impact as T07 — unauthorised charges and refunds against customer accounts.
column10: Mitigation is a secrets manager with short-lived credentials

column4: There is no tamper-evident audit log of what cart contents were sent to the model and what summary was returned.
column6: Absence of a control — the gap is near-certainly present with no audit log specified for the AI summarise step.
column8: Blocks dispute resolution for wrong summaries and regulatory explainability under GDPR Art. 22; complicates incident investigation.
column10: Only STRIDE-R threat in the list; absence of logging is a design gap that must be closed before launch
